What is the essential teaching in 'In the Context of the Deathless'?

In 'In the Context of the Deathless', the teaching opens with this observation: *"The first thing the Buddha said after deciding that he would teach was, “Open are the doors to the deathless."* The central invitation is to turn one's investigation inward — to verify the Dhamma not as a set of beliefs, but as directly observable reality in one's own body, speech, and mind. As the text teaches, the Dhamma is *akāliko* — ever-present — and *opanayiko* — leading inward — available to be known (*paccattaṁ*) by each practitioner for themselves. There is no need to search elsewhere; the truth is already here.

Why does 'In the Context of the Deathless' place such emphasis on contemplating the body?

The text teaches: *"The first thing the Buddha said after deciding that he would teach was, “Open are the doors to the deathless. Let those with ears show forth their conviction.” The first thing he said when he met with his first disciples was, “The deathless has been attained. I will instruct you. I will teach you th..."* Body contemplation (kāyagatāsati) is the Buddha's own recommended entry point because the body is always with us and plainly reveals the three characteristics: it is impermanent (anicca), involves stress (dukkha), and is not a self (anattā). Beginning with the five meditation themes — hair of head, hair of body, nails, teeth, skin — the practitioner trains the eye of discernment (paññā) to see through the illusion of beauty and find the inherent truth beneath. Right now, bring gentle attention to the feel of your body sitting — notice it is always changing.
